topic: Introduction to Religions (Two from the SL list)
subject: religious-studies

items.title: Paley's watchmaker argument was published in 1802

options.text: If we found a stone on a heath, we would infer no designer
If we found a watch on a heath, the complexity and purposive arrangement of its parts would compel us to infer a watchmaker — and similar reasoning applied to nature implies a divine designer
Nature is too random to need a designer
The argument compares the universe to a clockwork mechanism explicitly

items.reveal:
William Paley's 'Natural Theology' (1802) opens with the watch-on-the-heath analogy. He uses the human eye as his prime biological example.

Hume's 'Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion' (1779, published posthumously) anticipated and refuted versions of the design argument decades earlier — the analogy is weak (the universe is not like a watch), there are flaws (suggesting an apprentice designer or a committee), and the argument cannot reach a single benevolent God.

Darwin's 'On the Origin of Species' (1859) provided a non-design explanation for biological complexity. Modern Intelligent Design (Behe, Dembski, 1990s onwards) is a controversial attempt to revive the argument scientifically.
items.why: The design argument keeps returning in new forms. Each version has to deal with the next development in science — biological evolution, cosmic fine-tuning, multiverse cosmology — making it a moving target rather than a settled debate.

items.title: Kant gave multiple formulations of the categorical imperative
items.claim: How does Kant's categorical imperative work?

options.text: One simple rule: do unto others as you would have them do to you

Multiple formulations including universalisability ('act only according to that maxim by which you can at the same time will that it should become a universal law') and humanity-as-end ('act so as to treat humanity, whether in your own person or in that of another, always as an end, never as a means only')
Whatever maximises happiness is morally required
An empirical rule derived from observation

items.reveal:
Kant's 'Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals' (1785) sets out the categorical imperative. Standard count: three formulations.

Formula of Universal Law: 'Act only according to that maxim by which you can at the same time will that it should become a universal law.'
Formula of Humanity: 'Act so as to treat humanity, whether in your own person or in that of another, always as an end, never as a means only.'
Formula of the Kingdom of Ends: 'Act according to the maxims of a member of a merely possible kingdom of ends.'

The formulations are intended to be equivalent in extension but to emphasise different aspects. Kant's most famous example (lying to the murderer at the door) shows the strict reading: lying is universally impermissible.
items.why: Kantian ethics is sometimes reduced to 'don't lie' or 'universalise your action'. The multiple formulations and the humanity-as-end principle are richer — and more humane — than the slogan suggests.

items.title: Sikhism was founded in 1469 by Guru Nanak
items.claim: What was Guru Nanak's central teaching?

options.text: A synthesis of Hinduism and Buddhism

One God (Ek Onkar), equality of all people, honest work (kirat karna), sharing with others (vand chakna), remembrance of God (naam japna) — rejecting caste, ritualism and religious exclusivism of his time
A purely philosophical movement with no religious claims

items.reveal_title: There is neither Hindu nor Muslim
items.reveal:
Born in 1469 at Nankana Sahib (now in Pakistan), Nanak had a transformative spiritual experience in 1499. After emerging from three days at the Bein river he reportedly said 'There is no Hindu, there is no Muslim' — pointing past religious labels to a shared underlying truth.

He undertook four major journeys (udasis) across India, into Tibet, the Middle East and possibly to Mecca. He died in 1539.

The Mool Mantar — Sikhism's foundational statement — begins 'Ik Onkar': there is one God. The Guru Granth Sahib opens with this affirmation.
items.why: Sikhism is the youngest of the major Indian religions — a deliberate rethinking of religious identity in Mughal-era Punjab. Its founding moment is well-attested historically, unlike older religions.
